cards.title: Meet the computer — a helper, not a mystery
cards.takeaway: A computer is simply a smart tool that takes instructions from you, processes them, and shows you the result.
cards.body:
If you have ever used an ATM, a POS machine, or an Android phone, you have already used a computer!

Every computer does three simple jobs over and over:
- **Input:** You type or click to tell it what you want.
- **Processing:** Its inner brain works on your request.
- **Output:** It shows the answer on the screen or plays sound.

cards.title: Desktop vs. Laptop — same brain, different body
cards.takeaway: A desktop stays on one table with separate parts; a laptop folds all those parts into one portable book with a battery.
cards.body:
You will meet two main styles of personal computer:
- **Desktop computer:** Stays on a desk. The screen, keyboard, mouse, and main box sit separately and need constant power (or a UPS/inverter).
- **Laptop computer:** Folds shut like a notebook. Screen, keyboard, trackpad, speakers, and a rechargeable battery are all built into one light body you can carry in a bag.

check.prompt: Why can a laptop keep working for hours when NEPA takes light, while a basic desktop turns off immediately?

choices.text: A laptop does not use electricity at all
A laptop has a built-in rechargeable battery inside its body
A desktop has no processor inside it
Laptops only work when connected to Wi-Fi

check.hint: Think about what powers your phone when it is unplugged from the wall.
check.explanation: Exactly! A laptop packs a built-in rechargeable battery alongside its screen and keyboard, while a desktop relies on wall power or an external UPS/inverter.

cards.title: The 5 main parts you can see and touch
cards.takeaway: Monitor shows pictures, Keyboard types words, Mouse points and clicks, System Unit holds the brain, and Speakers play sound.
cards.body:
On a desktop setup, five everyday parts work as a team:
- **Monitor:** The TV-like screen that shows your work.
- **System Unit (the box):** The main case holding the **CPU** — the computer's **brain**!
- **Keyboard:** Keys for typing letters, numbers, and shortcuts.
- **Mouse:** Moves the arrow on screen so you can point, click, and scroll.
- **Speakers / Headphones:** Let you hear voices, alerts, and videos.

cards.title: Inside the System Unit — the real 'brain'
cards.takeaway: People sometimes call the whole box 'the CPU', but the true CPU is the tiny brain chip inside the System Unit.
cards.body:
In many Nigerian offices and cybercafés, people point at the big metal box on the desk and say *'turn on the CPU'*.

Now you know the friendly truth:
- The big box is the **System Unit**.
- Inside that box sits the **CPU (Central Processing Unit)** — the computer's **brain** that calculates, thinks, and runs every app you open.

check.prompt: Which part of the computer acts as its 'brain' that carries out instructions?

choices.text: The CPU inside the System Unit

check.hint: Monitor shows pictures and Mouse clicks — which part inside the box does the thinking?
check.explanation: Spot on! The CPU (Central Processing Unit) inside the System Unit is the computer's brain.

cards.title: Exploring the Windows Desktop
cards.takeaway: After signing in, you land on the Desktop — your home screen with app icons, the Taskbar at the bottom, and the Start button.
cards.body:
Once the computer turns on and you sign in, you see the **Windows Desktop**. Think of it like the top of a neat office table:
- **Icons:** Small pictures you double-click to open apps or folders.
- **Taskbar:** The long strip along the very bottom showing open apps and the clock.
- **Start Button:** The Windows logo at the bottom-left (or bottom-centre) where you open programs or shut down safely.

cards.title: How to turn ON and shut DOWN safely
cards.takeaway: Always shut down through Start → Power → Shut down — never pull the wall plug while the computer is running!
cards.body:
Turning **ON** is one press of the physical **Power button** (a circle with a small line `⏻`).

Turning **OFF** the right way protects your files:
1. Save any open work.
2. Click the **Start** button on screen.
3. Click **Power (⏻)** → **Shut down**.
4. Wait until the screen and lights go completely off.

**Warning:** Pulling the plug from the wall while Windows is running can corrupt your files and damage the drive!

check.prompt: What is the safest, correct way to turn off a Windows computer when you finish working?

choices.text: Pull the power cable straight out of the wall socket
Switch off only the monitor screen and walk away
Click Start → Power → Shut down and wait for it to power off
Hold down the spacebar for ten seconds

check.hint: Windows needs a few seconds to close open files neatly before power stops.
check.explanation: Correct! Using Start → Power → Shut down lets Windows save system state cleanly so no files get damaged.

cards.title: Using the mouse without tension
cards.takeaway: Left-click selects, double-click opens, right-click shows a helpful menu, and the wheel scrolls up and down.
cards.body:
Rest your hand gently on the mouse — no need to grip tightly!
- **Single left-click:** Selects an item or presses a button.
- **Double left-click (two quick taps):** Opens an icon or folder on the Desktop.
- **Right-click:** Opens a small menu of options for whatever you pointed at.
- **Scroll wheel:** Rolls pages up and down smoothly.

cards.title: Pressed Power and nothing happened? Check the basics first!
cards.takeaway: Before panicking, check wall power/switch, cable plugs at both ends, and the monitor's own power button.
cards.body:
If a friend says *'I pressed the power button and nothing happened'*, check the simplest things first:
1. **Wall socket & stabilizer/UPS:** Is the wall switch ON and is there power (or battery charge on a laptop)?
2. **Power cable:** Is the cord pushed firmly into both the wall and the back of the System Unit?
3. **Monitor power:** Sometimes the computer IS on, and only the monitor screen is switched off!

check.prompt: Your friend presses a desktop's power button and nothing lights up at all. What should you check FIRST?

choices.text: Check that the wall socket switch is ON and the power cable is firmly plugged in

check.hint: Always check electricity and cables before assuming anything inside is broken.
check.explanation: Yes! Nine times out of ten, a dead desktop simply has a switched-off wall socket, loose power cord, or turned-off UPS.
